name: The intellectual love of God (amor intellectualis Dei)
plain_explanation: As we come to understand more and more of reality as part of God, this growing understanding is itself accompanied by a special joy; this fusion of true thought and joy is what Spinoza calls the intellectual love of God, and he regards it as the highest human good.
precise_definition: A union of true understanding and joy that arises whenever the mind refers its ideas to God (i.e., understands them as part of the single, necessary whole); it is described as part of the infinite love with which God loves Himself.
why_it_mattered: It is Spinoza's substitute for personal immortality and conventional religious devotion, and the culminating good of the entire Ethics ('the mind's highest good is the knowledge of God').
historical_origin: Developed in Book V of the Ethics, following a geometrical proof-style demonstration that Russell quotes in full.
examples: Russell quotes Spinoza's geometrical 'proof' that 'love towards God must hold the chief place in the mind.'
objections: Russell notes a tension: Spinoza says God feels no pleasure or pain, yet also speaks of joy in the intellectual love of God; Russell suggests the 'joy' here may be something superior to ordinary pleasure.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Goethe admired the related proposition that one who loves God cannot want God to love him in return, though Russell says Goethe misunderstood it as self-abnegation rather than logical necessity.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Substitutes for the Christian promise of personal immortality: what is eternal in the mind is this intellectual love, not a personal afterlife.
